doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: New York work and early influences
title: Society band work in New York
summary: After moving to New York, Masso played society jobs for Lester Lanin, Peter Duchin and Meyer Davis; harmony formulas and professionalism.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Are we still rolling? All right. So after The World’s Greatest Jazz Band, which I assume by the way while you were playing with this you were able to still feed your four children?

Yes. Things got a little better every year. I eventually moved to New York so I was able to do work in the City. It took a while to establish myself, but I did all kinds of work there, Monk, I did society work, which I really can’t put down, I mean if it’s done well, why not do it?

Exactly. That’s who I worked for. I worked for Lester Lanin, I worked for Peter Duchin, I worked for the Meyer Davis office, and you know, first of all it paid very well and secondly the quality of musicianship in those groups is very high. And I’m a song player anyway. I grew up playing that kind of music with my dad, who had a band. And it’s very challenging when you get with the right people, playing harmony lines on a lot of those show tunes. There’s a formula that’s used. You know, the trombone player plays a certain line, the line above the melody; and the tenor sax player would be playing the line below the melody, so you don’t get in each other’s way. But it’s kind of a fun thing to do. I have a keyboard background, so that helps me a great deal as far as knowing harmony.
In the typical society orchestra, I would imagine that professionalism was really important also, that you had to learn to be on time, to look right.

Exactly. Take care of business. I mean you’d get there at least a half hour before the job starts, and just get on the stand and do what’s expected. You know, the griping, if you have to play a cha cha, play a good one. If you don’t like doing that stuff, don’t take the job.

Yeah, right. Well music, like you said, if it’s good, if it’s played well, if it’s played in tune, you don’t have to have it, that it’s the greatest thing in the world, that it’s my particular taste, but if you do it well it can still be enjoyable I would guess.
